t: Find Two Non-overlapping Sub-arrays Each With Target Sum
o: We need two disjoint contiguous subarrays, each summing exactly to `target`, minimizing the total of their lengths. In Example 1 the only candidates are the single elements `3` at indices 0 and 4, giving answer 2. In Example 2 three windows sum to 7; picking `[7]` (index 0) and `[7]` (index 3) avoids overlap and gives length 2. In Example 3 only one window sums to 6, so we return -1. Since `arr[i] >= 1`, all sums are strictly increasing as a window grows — this monotonicity is what makes sliding-window / one-pass techniques valid. With n up to 1e5, an O(n^2) enumeration of pairs of windows is too slow; we need roughly O(n).
k: Track, for each index i, the shortest valid subarray ending at or before i (`best[i]`); then any new target-sum window ending at i can pair with best[i - len] for O(1) answers.
Because all elements are positive, sliding-window expansion/shrinking cleanly finds every subarray with sum equal to target.
A left-to-right pass combining 'shortest window ending here' with 'best length so far' solves the problem in a single scan.

a.n: Approach 1: Prefix Sum Hash Map + Best-so-far DP
a.i: Use a hash map from prefix sum to its latest index to find, ending at each index i, the shortest subarray with sum = target: it starts right after the last occurrence of prefix(i) - target. Maintain `best` = minimum length of any valid subarray seen so far that ends before the current candidate's start. When a window [l..i] of length len is found, if best is finite, update answer with best + len; then update best with min(best, len). This guarantees non-overlap because best only counts windows ending before l.
s: Initialize map {0: -1}, running prefix sum, best = INF, ans = INF.
For each index i, add arr[i] to prefix.
If prefix - target exists in the map at index j, candidate length is i - j; if best < INF, set ans = min(ans, best + (i - j)).
Update best = min(best, i - j) for this found window.
Store map[prefix] = i (latest index keeps windows short); return ans if finite else -1.
a.t: O(n) expected — one pass with O(1) average hash-map operations.
a.sp: O(n) — the hash map may store up to n+1 distinct prefix sums.

a.i: Since all values are positive, a classic two-pointer window finds every subarray summing to target. Precompute `left[i]` = length of the shortest target-sum window entirely within arr[0..i]. Then scan again: whenever a window ends at i with start s, combine its length with the best window fully inside [0..s-1], i.e. left[s-1], updating the answer. This separates 'best on the left' from 'current window' explicitly.
s: First pass: sliding window over arr; when window sum equals target, record its length into left[end] and propagate left[i] = min(left[i-1], current) forward.
Reset window pointers and sum for a second pass.
Second pass: when window [s..i] hits sum target, if s > 0 and left[s-1] is finite, update ans = min(ans, left[s-1] + (i - s + 1)).
a.t: O(n) — each pointer moves forward at most n times across both passes.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 2 (sliding window + left-best array): it exploits positivity directly and is easy to explain; Approach 1 is equally optimal and slightly shorter to code. Key pitfalls: forgetting to check non-overlap (pairing only with windows strictly to the left), using the latest prefix index so windows stay minimal, and returning -1 when fewer than two disjoint windows exist. Edge cases: target larger than total sum, all-equal arrays like [1,1,...], and a single-element array. Follow-ups: handle negative numbers (then you must switch to prefix-sum hashing since sliding window breaks), or return the actual indices instead of lengths.
